title: AWS Storage Services: S3, EBS, EFS and Choosing the Right Storage Class
intro: AWS sells storage in three shapes: object storage (S3), block storage (EBS) and file storage (EFS and the FSx family), and each shape suits a different way of reading and writing data. This lesson teaches how each service works, how the S3 storage classes trade price against retrieval speed, and how to match a workload to the right service, class and lifecycle schedule.

sections.heading: Three storage types: object, block and file
sections.content:
Cloud providers sell storage in three shapes, and the shape decides how your software talks to the data. **Object storage** (Amazon S3) keeps whole files as objects in a flat namespace, and you reach them over HTTPS with simple API calls such as PUT, GET and DELETE. Think of a coat check: you hand over a coat, receive a ticket (the key), and later redeem the ticket for the whole coat. You never reach in and alter one sleeve. **Block storage** (Amazon EBS, Elastic Block Store) is a raw virtual disk. The operating system formats it with a file system and reads or writes individual blocks, exactly like the internal drive of a laptop. **File storage** (Amazon EFS and the Amazon FSx family) is a shared network drive: many machines mount the same directory tree over a protocol such as NFS or SMB, like the department file server in an office.

The table below is the single most useful comparison in the whole lesson. Most storage questions on the Cloud Practitioner exam, and most real design decisions, are answered by asking which of these columns fits.

| Property | Object (S3) | Block (EBS) | File (EFS / FSx) |
|---|---|---|---|
| How it is accessed | HTTPS API, lookup by key | Attached as a disk to an EC2 instance | Mounted over NFS or SMB by many clients |
| Unit of data | Whole object, up to 5 TB | Fixed-size block | Files and directories |
| Scope | Regional service, no size limit | One Availability Zone | EFS spans AZs in a Region; FSx depends on deployment type |
| Edit in place | No, you replace the whole object | Yes | Yes |
| Typical use | Media, backups, logs, data lakes, static sites | Boot volumes, databases | Shared content, home directories, CMS, HPC |
| You pay for | GB actually stored plus requests | GB provisioned plus performance | EFS: GB used. FSx: provisioned capacity |

A fourth option exists but is not durable: **instance store** is disk physically inside the host server. It is very fast, but its contents vanish when the instance stops or the host fails, so it only suits caches and scratch data.

**What is important to know:** durability and sharing differ per type. S3 is built to be the permanent home of data; EBS is tied to one AZ and normally one instance; file systems exist because several servers need the same files at once.

**What is important to ask** when a team requests storage: How will the software read the data (API, disk, or shared folder)? How many servers need it at the same time? Does it change in place or is it written once and read many times? How long must it outlive the server that created it? The answers choose the type before you ever look at price.

sections.heading: S3 fundamentals: buckets, objects, keys and the 11 nines
sections.content:
Amazon S3 (Simple Storage Service) is a regional object store with effectively unlimited capacity. Four terms carry most of the vocabulary. A **bucket** is the top-level container. Its name must be globally unique across all AWS accounts, and it lives in exactly one Region that you choose, based on latency to users, price and data residency rules. An **object** is the data plus its metadata, up to 5 TB each. The **key** is the object's full name, for example images/2026/logo.png. A **prefix** is the leading part of a key, here images/2026/. S3 has no real folders: the namespace is flat, and the console only draws folders by splitting keys on the slash character. That is why renaming a folder holding a million objects means copying a million objects, and why good key naming matters.

A single PUT can upload up to 5 GB; larger objects must use multipart upload (covered later). Since December 2020 S3 provides strong read-after-write consistency: after a successful write or delete, the next read sees the change, so you do not need to design around stale reads.

**The durability model.** S3 Standard is designed for 99.999999999% durability, the famous 11 nines. In practice this means that if you store 10 million objects you can expect to lose a single object roughly once every 10,000 years. AWS achieves this by storing redundant copies across a minimum of three Availability Zones (isolated groups of data centers inside a Region) and continuously verifying checksums. Every class except One Zone-IA uses this multi-AZ design.

**Durability is not availability.** Availability asks whether you can read the object right now. S3 Standard is designed for 99.99% availability, which is about 52 minutes of unreachable time per year. An object can be perfectly safe and still briefly unreachable. Durability also does not protect you from your own actions: an object you overwrite or delete is durably gone, which is the reason versioning exists.

**Cost model.** You pay for storage per GB-month, for requests (PUT, GET, LIST), for retrievals in the cheaper classes, and for data transferred out to the internet or to another Region. Data transferred in from the internet is free.

**Static website hosting.** A bucket can serve a static site (HTML, CSS, JavaScript, images) when you enable website hosting and name an index document. The website endpoint speaks HTTP only, so production sites put Amazon CloudFront in front for HTTPS and caching. It cannot run server-side code.

Who may read a bucket, how public access is blocked, and encryption for security are covered in the existing cloud storage security lesson; this lesson stays on what the services do and what they cost.

**What is important to ask:** Which Region must the data live in? Is the namespace designed so that keys can be listed by prefix? Does anyone confuse 11 nines of durability with a promise that nothing can be deleted?

sections.heading: S3 storage classes: matching price to access pattern
sections.content:
A storage class is a price and retrieval profile you assign per object. All classes keep the same 11 nines of design durability, so the real trade is among storage price, retrieval speed, retrieval fees and minimum commitments. The prices below are approximate us-east-1 list prices per GB-month and are only for comparing the classes; always check the current pricing page.

| Class | Best for | Retrieval time | Minimum storage duration | Approx. price per GB-month |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Standard | Frequently accessed, active data | Milliseconds | None | $0.023 |
| Intelligent-Tiering | Unknown or changing access | Milliseconds (frequent, infrequent and archive instant tiers) | None | $0.023 down to $0.004, plus a monitoring fee |
| Standard-IA | Infrequent access but needs speed | Milliseconds | 30 days | $0.0125 |
| One Zone-IA | Infrequent, easily re-created data | Milliseconds | 30 days | $0.01 |
| Glacier Instant Retrieval | Archive read about once a quarter | Milliseconds | 90 days | $0.004 |
| Glacier Flexible Retrieval | Archive read once or twice a year | Expedited 1-5 min, Standard 3-5 h, Bulk 5-12 h | 90 days | $0.0036 |
| Glacier Deep Archive | Compliance records kept for years | Standard within 12 h, Bulk within 48 h | 180 days | $0.00099 |

**How Intelligent-Tiering works.** S3 watches each object and moves it automatically: after 30 days without access it drops to the Infrequent tier, after 90 days to Archive Instant Access, and optional opt-in tiers (Archive Access, Deep Archive Access) go colder still. There are no retrieval fees and an accessed object returns to the Frequent tier. The cost is a small per-object monitoring charge (about $0.0025 per 1,000 objects per month), and objects under 128 KB are never tiered. It is the safe default when you cannot predict access.

**Pitfalls the exam and real bills both reward knowing:**

- **One Zone-IA stores data in a single Availability Zone.** It is cheaper because there is no multi-AZ copy, so losing that AZ loses the data. Use it only for secondary copies or data you can regenerate, never as the only copy of anything important.
- **Glacier Flexible and Deep Archive objects cannot be read directly.** You issue a restore request, wait minutes to hours, and receive a temporary copy for a number of days you choose. The restore is billed per GB and per request, and faster tiers cost more.
- **Minimum storage duration means early deletion is still billed.** Delete an object after 10 days in Standard-IA and you are charged for the remaining 20 days.
- **IA classes bill a minimum object size of 128 KB.** Millions of tiny files in Standard-IA can cost more than in Standard.
- **Retrieval fees on the IA and Glacier classes** punish a wrong guess. Archive data that is actually read weekly costs more than leaving it in Standard.

**What is important to ask:** How often will this be read, and how fast must it come back when it is? What happens to the business if it is lost or delayed? Can it be re-created? Those three answers pick the class.

sections.heading: S3 data management: versioning, lifecycle, replication and fast uploads
sections.content:
**Versioning** keeps every version of an object under the same key. Once enabled on a bucket you can suspend it but never fully remove it. Overwriting a key creates a new version; deleting a key without a version ID does not remove data but adds a **delete marker** that hides the object, and removing that marker restores it. Versioning is your protection against accidental overwrites and deletes. The price is that every version is billed as storage, so a file rewritten daily for a year becomes 365 stored copies unless you manage them.

**Lifecycle rules** automate that management. A rule applies to a whole bucket or to a filtered set (by prefix, tag or object size) and contains two kinds of action. A **transition action** moves objects to a cheaper class after a number of days. An **expiration action** deletes objects after a number of days. The class order is a one-way waterfall: Standard, then Standard-IA or One Zone-IA, then Glacier Instant, Flexible and Deep Archive. Objects must normally sit at least 30 days in Standard before transitioning to Standard-IA or One Zone-IA. Useful rule types include expiring noncurrent versions after a set number of days, removing expired delete markers, and **aborting incomplete multipart uploads** after a few days so abandoned upload parts stop costing money. Each transition is a billed request, so moving hundreds of millions of tiny objects has a real price.

**Replication** copies new objects automatically to another bucket. **Cross-Region Replication (CRR)** targets a bucket in a different Region, useful for lower latency to distant users, disaster recovery and compliance rules that require a second geography. **Same-Region Replication (SRR)** targets another bucket in the same Region, useful for aggregating logs, separating production and analytics copies, or keeping a copy in another account. Key facts:

- Versioning must be enabled on both the source and the destination bucket.
- Replication is asynchronous and applies to objects written after the rule is created; existing objects need S3 Batch Replication.
- Replication Time Control adds a service level of 99.99% of objects replicated within 15 minutes.
- You pay for storage in both buckets, replication requests, and for CRR the inter-Region data transfer, roughly 2 cents per GB. That cross-region bill surprises teams replicating many terabytes.

**Faster uploads.** **Multipart upload** splits a large object into parts of 5 MB to 5 GB (up to 10,000 parts) that upload in parallel and are stitched together at the end. It is recommended above 100 MB and required above 5 GB. If a part fails, only that part is retried, and the upload can pause and resume. **S3 Transfer Acceleration** sends uploads to the nearest CloudFront edge location, which then carries the data over the AWS backbone to the bucket. It helps when users are far from the bucket's Region, uses a special accelerate endpoint, and carries an extra per-GB fee. The two features combine: a user in Singapore uploading a 20 GB video to a bucket in Frankfurt benefits from both.

**What is important to ask:** What is the retention need for old versions? Which prefixes are hot versus cold? Does a second Region really need a copy, and who pays the transfer?

sections.heading: EBS in depth: volume types, snapshots and encryption at rest
sections.content:
Amazon EBS provides block volumes for EC2 instances. A volume lives in one Availability Zone and attaches to an instance in the same AZ, and the data persists independently of the instance, unlike instance store. Boot volumes are EBS volumes, and by default the root volume is deleted when the instance terminates unless you change DeleteOnTermination. Most volume types attach to one instance at a time. The exception is **Multi-Attach**, available on io1 and io2, which lets up to 16 Nitro instances in the same AZ share a volume for clustered applications. You pay for the capacity and performance you provision, whether you fill the disk or not.

The volume type decides performance and price. SSD types suit random reads and writes; HDD types suit large sequential streams.

| Type | Medium | Max IOPS | Max throughput | Size range | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| gp3 | SSD, general purpose | 16,000 | 1,000 MiB/s | 1 GiB to 16 TiB | Default for boot volumes, dev and test, most databases |
| io2 (Block Express) | SSD, provisioned IOPS | Up to 256,000 on supported instances (64,000 otherwise) | Up to 4,000 MiB/s | 4 GiB to 64 TiB | Critical databases, sub-millisecond latency, 99.999% durability |
| st1 | HDD, throughput optimized | 500 | 500 MiB/s | 125 GiB to 16 TiB | Big data, log processing, data warehouses |
| sc1 | HDD, cold | 250 | 250 MiB/s | 125 GiB to 16 TiB | Infrequently accessed data at the lowest EBS price |

**gp3 specifics.** Every gp3 volume starts at a baseline of 3,000 IOPS and 125 MiB/s regardless of size, and you can raise IOPS up to 16,000 and throughput up to 1,000 MiB/s independently of capacity. The older gp2 type tied IOPS to size (3 IOPS per GiB, with burst credits), so people bought oversized disks just to get speed. gp3 is also about 20% cheaper per GB, so migrating gp2 to gp3 is a classic cost saving. **io2** is for workloads where latency and consistency are worth paying for. Standard SSD volumes are designed for 99.8 to 99.9% durability, while io2 is designed for 99.999%. st1 and sc1 cannot be boot volumes.

**Snapshots.** A snapshot is a point-in-time backup of a volume, stored in S3 by the service (you do not see it in your own bucket list). The first snapshot copies all used blocks and later ones are **incremental**, saving only changed blocks, so deleting an old snapshot removes only data no newer snapshot needs. Snapshots are regional objects: you can restore one into a new volume in any AZ of the Region, or copy it to another Region for disaster recovery. A volume restored from a snapshot loads blocks lazily, so first reads can be slower unless Fast Snapshot Restore is enabled. Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager schedules snapshot creation and retention, and the Snapshot Archive tier cuts storage cost for snapshots you keep for months, with restore taking 24 to 72 hours.

**Encryption at rest** is a per-volume setting backed by AWS KMS keys. It encrypts the data on the volume, the snapshots made from it and the traffic between instance and volume, with negligible performance effect. Key policy and compliance detail belong to the cloud storage security lesson.

**What is important to ask:** Does this workload need IOPS, throughput or just capacity? Is it in the right AZ? Who deletes stale snapshots?

sections.heading: Shared file systems: EFS and the FSx family
sections.content:
Block volumes belong to one server. When several servers must read and write the same files at once, you need a **file system service**. The mental model is a managed office file server: you mount it, and AWS handles the hardware, patching and replication.

**Amazon EFS (Elastic File System)** is a managed NFS file system for Linux. Key characteristics:

- It is **elastic**: it grows and shrinks automatically as you add and remove files, and you pay for the GB actually used. There is no capacity to provision, unlike EBS.
- The standard design stores data redundantly across multiple Availability Zones in a Region, and each AZ has a **mount target** that instances connect to. Thousands of instances, containers and Lambda functions can mount it concurrently.
- It supports NFS v4.0 and v4.1 and is for Linux clients; Windows instances are not supported.
- It has storage classes with lifecycle management, like S3: Standard, Infrequent Access and Archive for multi-AZ data, plus One Zone variants that keep a single copy in one AZ at lower cost. Files not read for a set number of days move automatically to the cheaper class.
- Throughput modes (Elastic, Provisioned or Bursting) determine how performance scales with load.

Typical EFS uses: a web farm in three AZs sharing uploaded images or a content management system, shared home directories, build and CI artifacts, and container storage.

**Amazon FSx** is a family of managed file systems, each a specific well-known product that AWS runs for you. Choose by protocol and ecosystem:

| FSx flavor | Protocol | Choose it when |
|---|---|---|
| FSx for Windows File Server | SMB, Active Directory integration | Windows applications need shared folders, DFS and NTFS permissions |
| FSx for Lustre | Lustre parallel file system | High-performance computing, machine learning training, fast scratch space linked to S3 |
| FSx for NetApp ONTAP | NFS, SMB, iSCSI | You already run NetApp and want snapshots, cloning and multi-protocol access |
| FSx for OpenZFS | NFS | Migrating ZFS workloads with very low latency needs |

**Choosing among the four storage choices in an exam-style way:**

- Many Linux servers, shared files, no capacity planning: **EFS**.
- Windows file shares with Active Directory: **FSx for Windows File Server**.
- Supercomputer-style parallel processing reading huge datasets: **FSx for Lustre**.
- One database server needing a fast disk: **EBS**, not a file system.
- Billions of web objects served over HTTP: **S3**, not a file system.

A common mistake is to use EFS as a general replacement for EBS. A network file system adds protocol latency and costs more per GB than gp3, so a single-instance database belongs on a block volume. Equally, putting rarely read archives on EFS Standard when S3 or Glacier would store them for a fraction of the price is a cost trap.

**What is important to ask:** What protocol do the clients speak? Linux or Windows? Is the data mostly read from many places at the same moment?

sections.heading: Moving data in: Snowball, DataSync and Storage Gateway
sections.content:
Getting existing data into AWS is a storage problem of its own. The first calculation is arithmetic: 100 TB over a dedicated 1 Gbps link at full line rate takes about 9 days, and real links rarely sustain full rate, so a poor connection can mean months. The service you pick depends on volume, bandwidth and whether the link is a one-time move or permanent.

**AWS Snow Family (Snowball Edge)** is the offline option. AWS ships a ruggedized storage appliance to your site, you copy data to it locally, ship it back, and AWS loads it into S3. Snowball Edge Storage Optimized holds tens to hundreds of terabytes per device, data on it is encrypted, and the shipping carrier tracks it. Snowcone is a smaller device, and Snowmobile was a shipping container on a truck for exabyte-scale moves. Snow devices can also run EC2 instances and Lambda functions locally for edge processing in places with no connectivity. AWS has announced that the Snow family is closing to new customers and points to online tools, so check current availability, although the concept still appears in the Cloud Practitioner exam and in older environments. Rule of thumb: if the transfer would take more than about a week online, an offline device was historically the answer.

**AWS DataSync** is the online transfer service. You install an agent in your data center (or run it in AWS), point it at an NFS share, SMB share, HDFS or another object store, and it copies to S3, EFS or FSx on a schedule. It handles parallel transfer, bandwidth throttling, automatic retries and integrity verification, and AWS describes it as up to 10 times faster than hand-rolled open source tools. It is the right choice for recurring or ongoing migrations, such as a nightly sync, and for moving data between AWS storage services.

**AWS Storage Gateway** is a hybrid bridge for applications that stay on premises but need cloud storage behind them. A virtual or hardware appliance presents local protocols and stores data in AWS:

- **S3 File Gateway**: NFS and SMB shares whose files are stored as S3 objects, with a local cache for hot data.
- **Volume Gateway**: iSCSI block volumes backed by S3, with point-in-time snapshots stored as EBS snapshots.
- **Tape Gateway**: a virtual tape library for existing backup software, with tapes archived to S3 Glacier classes.

**AWS Transfer Family** is a related service that offers managed SFTP, FTPS and FTP endpoints in front of S3 or EFS, for partners who exchange files over those protocols.

| Situation | Service |
|---|---|
| Hundreds of TB, poor or no bandwidth, one-time move | Snow Family (check availability) |
| Recurring or ongoing copy from NFS or SMB to AWS | DataSync |
| On-premises apps need cloud-backed shares, volumes or tapes | Storage Gateway |
| Partners upload via SFTP | Transfer Family |

**What is important to ask:** How much data and how much bandwidth? Is it one-time or continuing? Must on-premises applications keep their current protocol?

sections.heading: Worked example: hot, warm and cold data for one workload
sections.content:
A mid-sized online retailer runs a web store in AWS. We will choose services and storage classes for its data, and justify each pick by access pattern, durability need and cost.

| Data | Service and class | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Product images, CSS and JavaScript served to shoppers | S3 Standard behind CloudFront | Read constantly, millisecond latency, no retrieval fee, no minimum duration |
| Customer-uploaded review photos | S3 Intelligent-Tiering | Popular right after upload, rarely viewed later, pattern unpredictable |
| Order database (single primary server) | EBS gp3 (io2 if latency proves critical), daily snapshots | Needs a fast disk, not a shared one; snapshots are the backup |
| Daily database dumps and app backups | S3 Standard for 30 days, then Standard-IA, then Glacier Flexible Retrieval | Restore is needed in the first weeks; after that almost never |
| Seven years of invoices and audit records | Glacier Deep Archive | Legally retained, read a few times a year at most, hours of waiting is acceptable |
| Shared template folder for 12 web servers in 3 AZs | EFS Standard | Many Linux servers need the same files at once |

**The lifecycle for the backup bucket.** Rule scope: the prefix backups/. Day 0: Standard (satisfies the 30-day minimum before an IA transition). Day 30: transition to Standard-IA. Day 90: transition to Glacier Flexible Retrieval. Day 365: transition to Glacier Deep Archive (the objects have been in Flexible well beyond its 90-day minimum). Day 2,555 (7 years): expire. Also on the bucket: abort incomplete multipart uploads after 7 days, and expire noncurrent versions 30 days after they are replaced.

**The cost logic.** Take 10 TB (about 10,240 GB) of backups. In Standard that is roughly 10,240 x $0.023 = $235 per month. In Deep Archive it is roughly 10,240 x $0.00099 = $10 per month. Leaving old data in Standard forever wastes about 95% of the money, and a lifecycle rule costs nothing to write. In the other direction, putting last night's backup directly into Deep Archive would be a mistake: a failed database at 9 a.m. would mean waiting up to 12 hours for Standard retrieval.

**Why not One Zone-IA?** The backups are the last line of defense, so storing them in a single AZ would risk losing them in the same event that destroyed production. One Zone-IA would be acceptable for thumbnails that the application can regenerate from the originals.

**Why not replicate everything cross-Region?** Replicating the backup bucket to a second Region doubles storage and adds about 2 cents per GB transfer, which is justified for the invoice archive (a regulatory disaster recovery requirement) but probably not for review photo thumbnails.

**Check yourself:** Suppose the company hosts a 4 TB video library and a quarterly analytics job reads 5% of it. Intelligent-Tiering saves money without retrieval fees if the 5% is unpredictable; Glacier Instant Retrieval wins if the job reads the same predictable set each quarter and millisecond access is required. Notice that the justification always names the access pattern first, then the price.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls and the questions an analyst asks
sections.content:
Storage mistakes are rarely dramatic. They show up as surprise bills, slow restores and lost copies. This final section collects the traps from the lesson in one checklist, so you can review a design in minutes.

**Pitfalls**

- **Confusing durability with availability.** 11 nines means data is not lost. It does not mean it is always instantly reachable, and it does not stop deletes.
- **One Zone-IA as the only copy.** One AZ failure removes the data. Use it only for regenerable or secondary data.
- **Glacier surprises.** Flexible and Deep Archive require a restore request, take minutes to 48 hours, and bill for retrieval. Do not archive data that someone reads weekly.
- **Minimum durations and sizes.** Early deletion and tiny objects in IA classes are billed as if the minimums applied.
- **Versioning without lifecycle.** Every overwrite becomes billed storage forever unless noncurrent versions expire.
- **Incomplete multipart uploads.** They are invisible in normal listings but still billed until aborted by a lifecycle rule.
- **Cross-Region replication cost.** You pay for a second copy plus inter-Region transfer. It needs a business reason.
- **EBS bought by size.** Paying for large gp2 disks to get IOPS, instead of gp3, wastes money. Unattached volumes and old snapshots keep billing after the server is gone.
- **Wrong type for the job.** A database on EFS or shared files on EBS (which attaches to one instance in one AZ) usually signals a design problem.
- **Slow online transfer.** Always calculate days at real bandwidth before choosing between DataSync and an offline device.

**Questions to ask for every data set**

1. How is it accessed: API, disk or shared folder?
2. How often, and how fast must it be returned?
3. What does losing it cost, and can it be re-created?
4. How long must it be kept, and when can it be deleted?
5. Which Region and Availability Zone does it need, and does a second copy elsewhere pay for itself?
6. Who owns the lifecycle, snapshot retention and cost review?

**A short decision flow.** If many servers share files, choose a file system. If one server needs a disk, choose EBS, and pick gp3 unless a measured need justifies io2 or HDD types. Otherwise it is probably an object, and you choose the S3 class by access pattern: Standard for hot data, Intelligent-Tiering when you cannot predict, Standard-IA for infrequent but fast, Glacier classes for archives, with a lifecycle rule that moves data down the waterfall as it cools. For security questions about who can reach the data and how it is encrypted, continue with the cloud storage security lesson.

quiz.question: A single EC2 instance runs a database that needs a steady 12,000 IOPS, but the data only occupies 200 GiB. The team wants the lowest cost that still meets the IOPS target. Which storage choice fits best?

options.label: An EFS file system in Elastic throughput mode mounted over NFS
A gp3 EBS volume with IOPS provisioned independently up to 12,000
An sc1 cold HDD EBS volume sized large enough to reach the target
An S3 Standard bucket accessed by the database through the API

quiz.explanation: A database on one server needs a block disk, and gp3 lets you raise IOPS up to 16,000 independently of capacity, so a small 200 GiB volume can reach 12,000 IOPS without buying extra space. EFS is a shared network file system with extra protocol latency and a higher price per GB, so it is not the economical choice for a single-instance database. sc1 is a cold HDD type limited to about 250 IOPS no matter how large it is, so it cannot reach the target. S3 is object storage accessed over an API and cannot serve as a database disk.

quiz.question: A company must retain seven years of audit records for legal reasons. The data is read perhaps once a year, and waiting up to half a day for a retrieval is acceptable. Which S3 storage class gives the lowest storage cost?

options.label: S3 Standard-IA, which keeps data in milliseconds-retrieval storage
S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval, which returns archive data in milliseconds
S3 One Zone-IA, which stores infrequently used data in one zone
S3 Glacier Deep Archive, with standard retrieval within about 12 hours

quiz.explanation: Deep Archive is the cheapest class, at roughly a tenth of a cent per GB-month, and its 12-hour standard retrieval and 180-day minimum suit records kept for years and rarely read. Standard-IA and Glacier Instant Retrieval pay for millisecond access that this workload does not need, so they cost several times more. One Zone-IA is also more expensive and keeps a single copy in one Availability Zone, which is a poor home for records with a legal retention requirement.

quiz.question: To save money, an engineer stores the only copy of weekly exported reports in S3 One Zone-IA. What is the main risk of this decision?

options.label: The data lives in a single Availability Zone, so losing that zone can lose the reports
The reports can only be read after a restore request that takes up to 12 hours
The reports cannot be deleted for 180 days because of the minimum duration
The reports are limited to 5 GB because the class does not support larger objects

quiz.explanation: One Zone-IA is cheaper precisely because it drops the multi-AZ redundancy, so a failure or loss of that one Availability Zone can destroy data that has no other copy. Reports in this class still return in milliseconds, so there is no restore wait; that behavior belongs to Glacier Flexible Retrieval and Deep Archive. The minimum duration for One Zone-IA is 30 days, not 180, and deleting earlier only adds a charge rather than blocking the delete. Object size limits are the same 5 TB per object as other classes.

quiz.question: A team turns on Cross-Region Replication from a bucket holding 2 TB of existing objects. Which statement is correct?

options.label: Existing objects are copied immediately and the transfer is free between Regions
Versioning must be enabled on both buckets, and cross-Region transfer is billed
Only the destination bucket needs versioning, and replication is fully synchronous
Replication works only between buckets that are in the same Region

quiz.explanation: Replication requires versioning on both the source and destination buckets, and CRR bills for the second copy of storage plus inter-Region data transfer, around 2 cents per GB. A new replication rule applies to objects written after it is created, so existing objects need S3 Batch Replication, and the copy is asynchronous rather than synchronous. Same-Region Replication is the same-Region variant, whereas cross-Region replication is the one that crosses Regions by definition.

quiz.question: Twelve Linux web servers spread across three Availability Zones must read and write the same upload directory at the same time, without anyone planning capacity. Which service fits?

options.label: One EBS gp3 volume attached to all twelve instances at once
Instance store on each server, synchronized by a nightly script
Amazon EFS, mounted through a mount target in each Availability Zone
S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval accessed through restore requests

quiz.explanation: EFS is a managed NFS file system that spans multiple Availability Zones, grows and shrinks automatically, and lets many Linux clients mount the same directory at once. An EBS gp3 volume lives in one AZ and attaches to one instance, so it cannot serve servers in three zones. Instance store disappears when an instance stops and cannot be shared, so a nightly script would still leave servers with different data. Glacier Flexible Retrieval is archive object storage that needs a restore wait and cannot act as a live shared directory.
